# Sets

::: {.callout-note}
## What is a set?

A [`set`](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#sets) is an *unordered* collection of *unique* and *immutable* objects.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What does it mean that sets are unordered collections?

By design, [`set`](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#sets) is a data structure with *undefined element ordering* (see Snippet 4.22 --- the outcome included in line 6 does not follow any particular order).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What does it mean that sets have unique items?

By definition, an item appears only once in a set, no matter how many times it is added (see Snippet 4.22, line 2 Vs. line 7).
:::

```python
# create a list
>>> L = ["a", "a", "b", "c", "c"]

# get a set from L
>>> S = set(L)
>>> print(S)
{"b", "a", "c"}
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why should I use sets?

Sets made this way support common mathematical set operations (see Snippet 4.23). Hence, they have a variety of applications, especially in numeric and database-focused work.
:::

```python
# create two sets
>>> X = set(["a", "b", "c"])
>>> Y = set(["c", "d", "e"])

# set difference
>>> X - X
set()
>>> X - Y
{"a", "b"}

# union
>>> X | Y
{"a", "b", "c", "d", "e"}

# intersection
>>> X & Y
{"c"}

# superset
>>> X > Y
False

# subset
>>> X < Y
False
```
